transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Linda Kenyon.
The Justice Department confirms it has launched a criminal probe into the Alaska Senate race,
where two Dan Sullivans appear on the ballot.
One is the incumbent Republican senator-seeking re-election.
The other is a retired teacher, who is listed as unaffiliated on the ballot.
The Trump administration contends Democrats recruited the retired teacher to create voter confusion.
Alaska U.S. attorney Michael Heyman explains why the department believes an investigation
is needed to look into this.
I'm not making any assumptions on whether a crime has been committed or not.
That's why we are conducting that thorough investigation.
Alaska's Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate, Mary Peltola, said she's deeply offended over
any accusations that she had anything to do with the appearance of the two Dan Sullivan
candidates on the ballot.
Well, voters like Ames Tonninson says, "Give Alaskans a little credit for knowing the difference."
I think if Alaskan voters can learn how to spell Lisa Murkowski to write her in, I think
we'll be able to keep two Dan Sullivans straight.
Another voter said Alaska's Supreme Court already decided the Sullivans are two separate
people, adding, "It's pretty much plain and simple."
The tech sell-off is deepening on Wall Street.
The Nasdaq closed yesterday with its worst month in over a year.
Here, Stephen Bissaha reports investors are questioning whether massive spending on AI
is worth the price.
These stock drops look even steeper when you zoom out to the past month.
Facebook's parent company, Meta, is down more than 15 percent.
Google's parent company, Alphabet, down more than 18 percent.
Intel down more than 45 percent.
This sell-off sped up as tech companies updated investors about the massive amounts of money
they are spending on AI, particularly on data centers.
As given investors sticker shock, other parts of the market are also feeling the sting of
high oil prices.
Crude oil futures are up, selling at more than $104 a barrel.
Stephen Bissaha, NPR News.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada is working to become the first associate member
of the European Union.
As Dan Carpentruck reports, Carney's statement came at the end of a two-day summit in Montreal.
It's still not clear exactly what an associate membership would look like, be called, or
if it comes with any price tags. Canadian and EU officials in Montreal did put the final
touches on a number of negotiations, as well as commitments to a new, deeper alliance.
In his closing remarks, Carney said they were working toward the deepest possible partnership,
which will be determined over the coming months.
He said the plan is to conclude negotiations in June of next year.
He will then join European Council meetings.
And in March, the European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and the Council President
will convene a meeting of EU commissioners and Canada's federal cabinet.
The new partnership will also be presented to the European Union and the Canadian Parliament
for a debate and a vote.
For NPR News, I'm Dan Carpentruck in Toronto.
You're listening to NPR.
Authorities in the Democratic Republic of Congo say more than 5,000 people have died
from Ebola in the Central African Nation.
As Michael Kologi reports, the country now has more than 10,000 confirmed cases of Ebola.
The Ebola death toll figures released yesterday by Congolese officials come as the United
Nations reports that over the last three months, thousands of people had crossed from Congo
into neighbouring South Sudan, reportedly due to fears regarding the outbreak.
Eight of Congo's 26 provinces have been affected by the disease, with many Ebola-related deaths
in the country occurring away from treatment centres.
Meanwhile, in Kenya, the country's government says it continues to strengthen Ebola surveillance,
while urging its citizens to observe health protocols.
Kenya has recorded nine cases of the disease and two deaths.
For NPR News, I'm Michael Kologi in Nairobi.
A century after his death, world-renowned escape artist Harry Houdini continues to garner
attention.
In a rare essay written by Houdini, which has now been published, it sheds some light
on early influences in his life.
Houdini, who was born Eric Wides, became an international celebrity known for his escape
acts.
His mysterious death occurred on Halloween in 1926 and still remains a matter of debate.
Centennial events this weekend include the Grand Houdini Centenarium in Budapest and
an auction in Hollywood.
I'm Linda Kenyon, NPR News, in Washington.

topics.text: Justice Department opens criminal probe into Alaska Senate race over two Dan Sullivans on ballot
Tech stocks sell off on Wall Street as investors question massive AI spending; oil tops $104 a barrel
Canada's Mark Carney says Canada seeks associate membership in the European Union after Montreal summit
Congo reports more than 5,000 Ebola deaths and over 10,000 confirmed cases; Kenya logs nine cases
New essay by Harry Houdini published as centennial of his 1926 death is marked with events
